title: Multi-region surge control and graceful degradation for downstream stores
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Context:
We routinely see tail-latency and cascading errors during cross-region traffic spikes when downstream stores (Redis clusters for KV, Kafka for ingest, and Postgres for metadata) saturate their connection pools or experience increased p99 latency. Current fallback behavior is brittle: requests either block for connection timeouts or fail hard, causing SLO violations and noisy alerts.

Goal:
Implement a predictable, region-aware degradation strategy that keeps high-priority traffic within SLOs by combining: adaptive connection admission, tiered circuit-breakers per downstream type, fast-path degraded reads for non-critical flows, and a shadow/rollout for thresholds. This should reduce customer-facing errors during regional overload and provide observability hooks for debugging and postmortems.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Connection admission controller: per-tenant and per-region admission tokens backed by a lightweight in-memory budgeter. Tokens refill based on configured QPS and current observed downstream latency to bound concurrent connections and avoid head-of-line blocking.
2) Tiered circuit-breakers: implement separate circuits for Redis/Kafka/DB with three states (Closed, Degraded, Open). Transition rules driven by short-window p95/p99 and error-rate; Degraded allows limited degraded reads or hedged requests to fallback caches, Open rejects low-priority requests.
3) Degraded read path: for Redis and Postgres, provide an approx-read API that returns cached/expired data (with provenance metadata) or a small synthesized response for non-critical endpoints (e.g., hints in embeddings metadata).
4) Priority lanes and admission: distinguish high-priority lanes (interactive API requests) vs background/low-priority jobs (batch ingestion, async audits). Admission controller enforces watermarks so high-priority keeps passing when degraded.
5) Multi-region failover policy: when a region's downstream shows systemic degradation, automatically route eligible traffic to warm-read replicas in other regions (hedging + rate-limited spillover) while maintaining per-region cost and data consistency guards.
6) Observability & SLOs: emit fine-grained events: admission drops, circuit transitions, degraded-read counts, hedged-fanout rates. Add dashboards and alerts keyed by tenant, region, and downstream type.

Trade-offs and considerations:
- Complexity: introduces several runtime checks and policy knobs. We'll keep default policies conservative and provide telemetry-driven autotune later.
- Data staleness: degraded-read returns may be stale; callers must surface provenance and allow clients to opt into reduced guarantees.
- Cross-region cost: routing to other regions increases egress/cost and potential tail; we will rate-limit spillover and prefer read-only replicas.
- Testing: critical to test chaos scenarios and stale-data cases; shadowing will be used before full rollout.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Spike (1 week): prototype in the serving runtime a simple admission token bucket + per-downstream circuit component and integration tests against a Redis test harness.
- Implementation (3 sprints): integrate admission controller into connection pool layer, add circuit manager with state machine, implement degraded-read pathway and priority lanes.
- Telemetry (parallel): add metrics and traces for all transitions; build dashboards and alerting playbooks.
- Staged rollout (2 weeks): shadow mode in canary region, follow with gradual enablement per-region and per-tenant with feature flagging.

Acceptance criteria:
- The admission controller can limit concurrent downstream connections per-tenant within configurable thresholds and exposes metrics for drops and retries.
- Circuits correctly transition based on SLI inputs and public metrics show reduced error-rate spikes during simulated overloads by >=40%.
- High-priority interactive requests maintain configured latency SLOs (p95) during injected downstream failures while low-priority requests are shed.
- Degraded-read responses carry provenance headers and are opt-in by API route; docs updated.
- Playbook and dashboards in console are live; runbook steps documented for on-call.

Rollout and testing plan:
- Unit tests for state transitions and admission logic; integration tests with Redis/Kafka/Postgres emulators.
- Fuzzing and chaos experiments in staging: connection pool saturation, increased p99 latency, partial region blackhole.
- Canary shadow for 48h in a non-critical region with telemetry comparisons.
- Gradual ramp with feature flags and tenant opt-in; automatic rollback if degradation of customer-visible SLOs detected.

Documentation & links:
- Design doc (internal): https://drive.redwood.ai/downstream-resilience/design-adm-circuit
- Runbook draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/runbooks/downstream-degrade-playbook
- Staging chaos dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd1234/downstream-chaos
- Spike PR (proto): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1567

Open questions:
- Should degraded-read be a first-class API flag, or handled transparently with provenance headers? Recommend first-class opt-in per route for safety.
- Exact thresholds for transitions: start conservative and add autotune (shadow) to pick defaults.
- Tenant fairness: how to balance multi-tenant bursty workloads vs single-tenant high-throughput customers? May need per-tenant caps + global pool.

Next steps:
- Complete spike and demo to SRE and Platform leads (owner: Luca Martinez).
- Iterate on thresholds from spike telemetry and finalize acceptance criteria for canary rollout.
acceptance_criteria: Admission controller enforces per-tenant/concurrent connection limits and reports drops
Circuit state machine triggers on p95/p99 latencies and error rates
High-priority lane preserves p95 latency SLOs during downstream overload tests
Degraded-read responses include provenance and are documented as opt-in
Dashboards and runbook created and validated with on-call
